name: uthash
workload: Third-party C/C++ hash-table benchmark (uthash v2.3.0 vs std::unordered_map among 15 tables): tables grown to 20,000,000 keys at max load factor 0.875 with a shared MurmurHash3-finalizer/FNV-1a hash, measuring insert, erase and replace of existing keys, erase and lookup of existing and nonexisting keys, and iteration, for three key/value shapes (32-bit/32-bit, 64-bit/448-bit, 16-char string/64-bit).
claimed_speedup: Article text: "uthash's iteration is about twice as fast as std::unordered_map's iteration (albeit still extremely slow)". Heatmap for 0-20M keys (total time relative to the fastest table, std::unordered_map vs uthash): iterate 87.83 vs 37.39 (32-bit keys), 24.67 vs 10.53 (64-bit key/448-bit value), 79.94 vs 30.64 (string keys), i.e. 2.3-2.6x (derived from page data); erase existing 11.26 vs 7.79, 9.84 vs 6.10, 3.21 vs 2.41, i.e. 1.3-1.6x (derived from page data); erase nonexisting 5.25 vs 3.72, 5.83 vs 3.91, 2.43 vs 1.93, i.e. 1.3-1.5x (derived from page data); lookup nonexisting 3.67 vs 3.22, 3.96 vs 3.24, 2.32 vs 1.83, i.e. 1.1-1.3x (derived from page data); insert 64-bit/448-bit 4.91 vs 4.11 and string 2.87 vs 2.61 (1.1-1.2x, derived from page data). uthash is NOT faster for 32-bit-key insert (6.75 vs 6.39), 32-bit and 64-bit/448-bit replace (3.80 vs 2.71, 2.90 vs 2.34) or 32-bit lookup of existing keys (2.58 vs 2.28).
compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2.0 via MinGW-w64, C++20, -O3 -DNDEBUG (README build line: g++ -I. -std=c++20 -static -O3 -DNDEBUG -Wall -Wpedantic main.cpp)
tradeoffs: Macro-based intrusive hash table: every item embeds a 56-byte UT_hash_handle (per the benchmark article), node-based separate chaining like std::unordered_map, rudimentary API with the user writing much of the scaffolding. By default keys are hashed and compared byte-by-byte, which is unsafe for structs with padding bytes. Pure C, single header, BSD-1-Clause.
caveats: The numbers are a third-party comparison; uthash's own repo carries no benchmarks and never claims to beat std::unordered_map. The article's author concludes uthash 'should be avoided due to all-around poor performance' (it is far slower than open-addressing tables) and says its comments about std::unordered_map's poor performance also apply to uthash; the win over std::unordered_map is mixed. Heatmap figures are totals over the 0-20M-key run normalized to the fastest table, and the ratios here are derived from them. In the 0-200,000-key run (docs/result_2024-05-28T04_06_21.csv) uthash is slower than std::unordered_map for most insert, lookup and replace cases (for example 32-bit lookup of existing keys at N=200,000: 35,300 vs 15,700 in the CSV's time units, 2.25x slower, derived from CSV data), while at N=200,000 its iteration is faster only for the 64-bit/448-bit and string keys (derived from CSV data). Benchmarked version is uthash v2.3.0; the repo is now at v2.4.0. Run on Windows with MinGW-w64, so libstdc++ behaviour (including std::unordered_map growth policy) is specific to that build. The published article lives on github.io, which was blocked here; the numbers were read from the article source docs/index.md in the benchmark repo.

name: Wirehair
baseline: CM256 (catid/cm256, O(N^2) Cauchy-matrix MDS Reed-Solomon codec; Longhair measured alongside)
workload: Erasure-code encode and decode throughput for 128 data pieces of 64,000 bytes with 128 recovery pieces (code rate 1/2), WH256 (Wirehair with the GF256 inner loops) vs CM256, Longhair, FEC-AL and Leopard, on the author's AVX2 laptop.
claimed_speedup: Leopard's Benchmarks.md: WH256 wirehair_encode(N = 128) 661.644 MB/s and wirehair_decode 830.103 MB/s vs CM256 encode 99.6658 MBps and decode 104.651 MBps (Longhair 100.342 and 96.3757 MB/s), i.e. about 6.6x faster encode and 7.9x faster decode than CM256 (derived from page data). Text: Wirehair 'Encodes at 660 MB/s, and decodes at 830 MB/s for ALL cases' and is the fastest decoder in that comparison; Wirehair's README also states it scales as O(N) rather than O(N log N) (Leopard) or O(N^2) (Fecal).
hardware: Author's 'few year old' laptop with AVX2 (CPU model not stated)
tradeoffs: Not an MDS code: needs N + 0.02 packets on average and sometimes N + 1 or N + 2 (Benchmarks.md says about a 3% chance of one extra block). Rateless fountain code for large block counts (up to 64,000). Same page shows Leopard encodes about 3x faster (1.96 GB/s) at k=m=128, and the Fecal README shows FEC-AL encoding about 2x faster than Wirehair at N=1000 with about 100 losses and 4x faster with about 30 losses (Wirehair decodes about 2x faster at 100 losses, but 2x slower at 30). The Wirehair README itself calls it a pretty inefficient codec for N below about 128 compared with Fecal. Public C API; versioned wire profiles in the current tree.
caveats: First-party numbers from the same author as CM256, 'not being very rigorous' on one laptop, with no CPU model, compiler or flags, and one configuration (k=m=128, 64 KB pieces). The measured code is catid/wh256, a pre-production GF256 branch, not necessarily the current catid/wirehair tree. The numbers sit in the Leopard repo, not Wirehair's. Reed-Solomon (MDS, practical only up to 255 pieces) and a fountain code are not like-for-like. Baseline is the author's own CM256 rather than Jerasure, ISA-L or Zfec, and the author notes CM256's inner loops could still be improved with GF256. Wirehair's own README benchmarks only compare Wirehair 1 with Wirehair 2 (GCC 13.3, Threadripper PRO 9985WX) and show WH2 slower at 64-byte blocks, so they are no evidence against an outside baseline. Category erasure-codes is not one of the wave categories; filed under compression-and-encoding as the nearest domain.
